references.text: Isaiah's prophecy about the suffering servant who was mistreated but did not open his mouth—like a lamb led to slaughter. Jesus' silence before Herod fulfills this prophetic image ([ref:Jes 53:7|Isaiah 53:7]).

Jesus also said nothing in response to the charges against him before Pilate, which amazed the governor. This shows a consistent pattern where Jesus chose to remain silent toward his accusers ([ref:Matt 27:12-14|Matthew 27:12-14]).
Mark reports that Jesus gave no answer to Pilate's question, leaving Pilate amazed. Jesus' silence is a common feature in all the passion narratives ([ref:Mark 15:4-5|Mark 15:4-5]).
During the trial before the Sanhedrin, Jesus remained silent and did not answer when the high priest questioned him about the testimony brought against him ([ref:Mark 14:60-61|Mark 14:60-61]).
In John's account as well, Pilate questions Jesus, but Jesus gives him no reply. This highlights Jesus' deliberate silence toward earthly authorities ([ref:Joh 19:9|John 19:9]).

Herod had long wanted to see Jesus and hoped to witness him perform a sign. Jesus' silence in verse 9 is the direct response to Herod's curiosity and many questions described here ([ref:Luk 23:8|Luke 23:8]).
Philip refers to Isaiah 53:7–8 about the suffering servant who did not open his mouth—a passage read by the Ethiopian eunuch, understood as a prophecy concerning Christ ([ref:Apg 8:32|Acts 8:32]).

Peter writes that when Christ was insulted, he did not retaliate with insults; and when he suffered, he made no threats but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. Jesus' silence before Herod is an example of this attitude ([ref:1 Pet 2:23|1 Peter 2:23]).
